paras: The Atlanta Garfield memorial riot was a clash on September 26, 1881, in which police, U.S. Fifth Artillery soldiers and white citizens clubbed and wounded Black people outside DeGive's Opera House in Atlanta, Georgia, during memorial services for President Garfield. Police arrested a dozen to twenty Black men, and a crowd that tried to rescue them was charged and dispersed. Papers reported it as a riot that disgraced a funeral occasion, and they disagreed on its cause and on whether anyone died.

The services were held by the Coeur de Lion Commandery of the Knights Templar, with a procession that included the Fifth Artillery, the City Council, local military, a battalion of colored military and several lodges of colored Odd Fellows. According to a New Orleans special, at least thirty thousand people, more than half of them Black, gathered on Marietta Street, and the Opera House could not hold a tenth of them. The Ottawa Free Trader wrote that excluded Black people complained of "gross partiality and injustice" toward their race in the distribution of tickets.

While the exercises went on upstairs, a colored Odd Fellow who could not get in kicked over a stack of guns, and a soldier of the Fifth Artillery clubbed him with his musket. The Atlanta Post-Appeal, as quoted by the New York Sun, said the Fifth Artillery then "fell upon" a crowd of Black people "with swords and bayonets and clubs." The Savannah Morning News gave a different start: Black men pushed white ladies off the sidewalk, and when police interfered the crowd knocked over the Artillery's stacked arms and tried to use them on the police.

Soon afterward a police captain tried to arrest a Black man who swung at him and struck a white woman; the officer clubbed him, and soldiers and citizens wounded "several negroes" while keeping back the crowd. A New York wire said police "used their clubs dexterously" and arrested about twenty men, while the Savannah report counted a dozen or more.

At the Pryor Street station a Black man threw a rock that knocked down a white man, and a crowd formed nearby to rescue the prisoners, urged on by a man with a butcher knife. Police, reinforced by "many armed citizens," charged the crowd, captured the speaker and dispersed it "without firing a shot." The wire reported that many people were wounded in the rescue attempt.
Later, on Decatur Street, colored militia soldiers bayoneted a white man in the hand during a dispute over a wagon, and fights went on into the night.

That night the guard house was full and the street outside was crowded with the prisoners' friends, who, the Savannah correspondent wrote, swore "to have justice or more trouble." Mayor English urged the crowd to go home, and Adjutant General Baird stood ready to call out the military. The wire said the excitement had subsided by midnight; no report of trials appears in the coverage.

Coverage came from white papers, beginning with a Savannah Morning News report headed "Disorderly Negroes Create a Tumult" that called the prisoners "colored rioters" and warned of "serious trouble as to equal rights." The New York wire ran in Washington as "Riot in Atlanta, Ga." and in Dallas as "Nearly a Riot in Atlanta," printing the crowd as 25,000 in one and 45,000 in the other. The Louisiana Capitolian printed the New Orleans Democrat special twice under "A Difficulty Between Whites and Blacks," calling the rescuers "the mob."

In October northern papers took the story up, the Ottawa Free Trader calling the services "disgraced by a shameful riot." The New York Sun quoted the Post-Appeal's description of "a comedy of errors" and its view that the trouble came from "mixing the two races in the procession," which the Sun called a "somewhat queer moral."

Accounts gave four causes: pushing white women off the sidewalk, an assault on police, an Odd Fellow kicking over guns, and an attempt by excluded Black people to force the doors. The Colfax Chronicle reported that U.S. regular troops wounded several Black people, two fatally, while the Ottawa Free Trader said no one was killed and the fuller reports mention no deaths.

bases: The force against Black people in the crowd came from police with clubs, soldiers of the U.S. Fifth Artillery with muskets, swords and bayonets, and citizens aiding them (A2, A4, A8), in a street clash that began, by every account, with a Black man's act or an attempt to keep Black people back (A1, A4, A6).

A Savannah correspondent (A1), a New York wire (A2), a New Orleans special (A4) and the Atlanta Post-Appeal as quoted by the Sun (A8) independently agree on a clash between Black people, police and the Fifth Artillery at the Opera House during the Garfield services, though they differ on its cause and casualties.

accounts.label: Savannah Morning News correspondent
accounts.gist: White ladies were pushed off the sidewalk by colored men; when police interfered the Black crowd knocked over the Fifth Artillery's stacked arms and tried to use them on the police, and the Artillery joined a 'desperate fight' ending in a dozen or more arrests.

accounts.label: New York wire (Atlanta special)
accounts.gist: A colored man assaulted police keeping back the crowd; police clubbed and arrested about twenty leaders, and a rescue attempt at the jail left many wounded.

accounts.label: New Orleans Democrat special
accounts.gist: An Odd Fellow who could not get in kicked over a stack of guns and was clubbed by a soldier; soldiers and citizens wounded several Black people; police and armed citizens charged a crowd forming to rescue prisoners near the Pryor Street station.

accounts.label: Ottawa Free Trader
accounts.gist: Black people excluded from the Opera House, who said tickets had been distributed unfairly against their race, tried to force the doors; both colors were wounded and no one was killed.

accounts.label: Atlanta Post-Appeal (via the Sun)
accounts.gist: An artilleryman clubbed a 'sable Odd Fellow' who knocked down guns, and the Fifth Artillery fell on a yelling crowd with swords, bayonets and clubs; the paper blamed mixing the races in the procession.

accounts.label: Colfax Chronicle
accounts.gist: Several Black people were wounded, two fatally, by U.S. regular troops.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News headlined 'Disorderly Negroes Create a Tumult', called the prisoners 'colored rioters' and warned of 'serious trouble as to equal rights'.
The wire ran as 'Riot in Atlanta, Ga. Trouble Between Colored People and Policemen' and 'Nearly a Riot in Atlanta', praising police who 'used their clubs dexterously'.
The New Orleans special, headed 'A Difficulty Between Whites and Blacks', blamed an angry Odd Fellow and an 'unruly negro' and called the rescue crowd 'the mob'.
The Ottawa Free Trader called the day 'disgraced by a shameful riot' but reported the excluded Black people's complaint of 'gross partiality and injustice' in ticket distribution.
The Sun relayed the Post-Appeal's 'comedy of errors' with irony, calling its race-mixing explanation a 'somewhat queer moral'.
